chapter_theme: The worth of an action lies in its cleanness: no gain, necessity or even a mother's hunger justifies what the worthy condemn, because tainted gain departs as it came and leaves ruin behind.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the excellence of clean action (651), the instruction not to do what brings sin and blame (652-656), and the reasons (657-660).

651.reading: Good companions bring prosperity, while good action brings everything one could want.
651.nuance: The verse does not say what 'everything' includes. Parimelazhagar expands it to virtue, wealth and pleasure here and desired stations hereafter, and he frames the contrast as between the visible good of allies and the inferred good of deeds.

652.reading: One must at all times avoid action that yields neither renown nor good.
652.nuance: என்றும் is pointed. Parimelazhagar says it holds in rising, shrinking and stable circumstances; Manakkudavar says it holds even when one has no means of doing anything else. The rule doesn't relax under pressure.

653.reading: Those who say 'we shall rise' must refrain from the deed that dims their light.
653.nuance: Ambition itself is the ground of the restraint. Parimelazhagar's summary is that gain that dims one's light isn't gain.

654.reading: Even when caught in trouble, those of unshaken clarity won't do what is degrading.
654.nuance: Pope's 'ever-during vision' suggests mysticism; the Tamil நடுக்கற்ற காட்சி is steadiness of judgement. Parimelazhagar's reasoning is a calculation: trouble passes but disgrace doesn't, and what must come will come anyway.

655.reading: Do nothing that makes you cry out 'What have I done!'; but if you do, it's good not to do the like.
655.nuance: The second line turns on what அன்ன points to. Pope gives both answers: his couplet says sin no more, and his gloss says do not grieve.

positions.position: Once done in confusion, don't go on grieving: regret displays a lack of remedy and firmness and spreads one's own shame. He says all others miss the connection.
If one acts at all, one should not do anything like such deeds.
Having done it, the good thing is not to continue it.

656.reading: Even if you must watch the mother who bore you go hungry, don't do what the worthy condemn.
656.nuance: The verse picks the hardest case it can imagine and refuses the exception. Its reach is the dispute.

positions.position: This overrides a general dharma rule permitting wrong to feed aged parents, wife and infant, but only for ministers, who have standing and royal duties.
positions.quote: தீயன பலவுஞ் செய்தாயினும் புறந்தருக' என்னும் அறநூற்பொது விதி

positions.position: It applies to anyone, with no exception: not even to relieve a mother in the throes of hunger.

657.reading: The utter poverty of the worthy is above wealth gained under a load of blame.
657.nuance: Manakkudavar sees this as a reply to an objection: living by these rules will leave you poor. The verse concedes it. Poverty is not denied or softened by கழி, 'extreme'.

658.reading: Even when they succeed, the forbidden things people do without shunning them bring anguish.
658.nuance: முடிந்தாலும் answers the practical objection that the end might come off. Parimelazhagar goes further and doubts it: such acts won't usually succeed, and even if somehow they do, pain follows.

659.reading: All that is taken with tears leaves with tears; what comes from good ways, even if lost, pays later.
659.nuance: The verse names no one in அழ. The commentators divide the tears, so the victim weeps on taking and the taker on losing, and this moral symmetry is part of the sound of the line. பின் covers the next birth for Parimelazhagar, which the verse does not specify.

660.reading: Making wealth by deceit and feeling secure in it is like pouring water into an unfired clay pot.
660.nuance: Both pot and water are lost: the wrongly got wealth also destroys the one it was meant to protect.

positions.position: ஏமார்த்தல் means making the king safe with such wealth. He attacks those who read it as rejoicing, since that breaks the simile's form.
positions.quote: பிறரெல்லாம், 'ஏமாத்தல்' என்று பாடமோதி, அதற்கு மகிழ்தல் என்றும்

positions.position: It means delight: one enjoys what one gained by deception, and both person and wealth perish.

links.note: 69 gives a mother's greatest joy as hearing her son called சான்றோன், greater than at the birth. 656 uses the same two words, ஈன்றாள் and சான்றோர், and places that standing above her hunger. Read together, the son's choice could be seen as what she would have wanted, though neither verse says so.

1041 says nothing hurts like poverty. 657 chooses extreme poverty over tainted wealth. The chapter on poverty doesn't withdraw this, so the choice is made in full knowledge of what the poverty will be.
Both state a return of harm: 319 in morning and evening, 659 in the taking and the leaving. 659 restricts it to wealth and adds the positive half, that clean gains come back.

source_issues: 651: The verse reads த்ருஉம், a typographical error for தரூஉம் (as in Parimelazhagar's lemma).
653: The verse reads ஒஓதல் for ஓஒதல், and Parimelazhagar glosses ஓதல் as a shortened form of ஓவுதல்.
